newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: IMF official gives upbeat assessment of Colombia.
newsitem.headline: IMF official gives upbeat assessment of Colombia.

text.p: A senior International Monetary Fund official said there are signs that Colombia's economy is returning to the path of solid growth after last year's slowdown.

But Paulo Neuhaus, the IMF's division chief for Central and South America, cautioned that the government must take further steps to rein in public spending to ensure that growth will continue over the medium and long term.
"There is a recovery in economic activity that is very positive," Neuhaus said in an interview with Colombia's Radionet radio news program.
"What we've been discussing with the authorities are the necesssary corrections so that this recovery will be sustainable," he said.

Neuhaus granted the rare interview after a three-week fact-finding visit to Colombia, which suffered a sharp slowing in economic growth last year amid the political crisis stemming from charges that President Ernesto Samper financed his 1994 election campaign with drug money.

Bogota's El Espectador newspaper, citing figures from the National Planning Department, reported earlier this week that Colombia's gross domestic product grew by an anemic 2.1 percent in 1996, roughly in line with population growth.
The figure, in a country where growth has averaged 4.5 percent over the last decade, would be the lowest since 1991.
Neuhaus said the IMF and government officials agreed that important steps have been taken recently to cut fiscal expenditures.

But he stressed the IMF's view that there is a need for further public spending cutbacks to get the government's economic house in order and slash a burgeoning fiscal deficit running at about 4 percent of GDP.
"Beyond the short-term outlook, there are potential problems stemming from the increase in public spending, which has been growing a lot in the last few years," he said.
"It's important to attack medium and long-term structural fiscal problems such as decentralization and potential deficits in the social security system," he added.

He did not elaborate, but central bank officials have criticized the government's longstanding practice of financing of its fiscal deficit with money generated by the financially- troubled Social Security Institute, the government retirement and health fund.

Neuhaus said Washington's decertification of Colombia as an ally in the drug war would have little effect on Colombia's return to growth in 1997, since "capital markets have discounted that factor." He conceded that it could serve as a "psychological obstacle" to some private investment flows, however.
Neuhaus described Colombia's outlook as "quite positive" overall.

But he noted that the government faces "important challenges," especially after this week's collapse of its three-month-old economic emergency plan. The plan, aimed at trimming the deficit by shoring up tax revenues and fighting tax evasion, was ruled illegal by a high court on grounds that the government abused special powers in imposing taxes by decree.

To counteract the court ruling, the government announced Thursday that it was temporarily raising its import tariffs. Neuhaus warned that this could create problems with Colombia's trading partners and with the World Trade Organization.
